summary: Three-part history of vaccine refusal, from 19th-century riots and racist smallpox campaigns in Britain and the US to Andrew Wakefield's fraudulent 1998 MMR-autism study and pediatrician Bob Sears profiting from the fear it created.

evidence.note: Jenner presents cowpox vaccination to the Royal Society in 1796
First anti-vaccination society formed in Boston around 1798, before US vaccinations began
Stockholm vaccine refusal and the 1874 epidemic
Leicester mass march and the Royal Commission leading to conscientious objector exemptions
Smallpox framed as a Black disease; racist quarantines and forced vaccinations in the US South
Lora Little edits The Liberator and leads anti-compulsion campaigns
Homeopaths and botanical physicians lead the anti-vaccine side of the medical war
1905 Supreme Court ruling upholds compulsory vaccination
Wakefield patents a test and a single measles vaccine and seeks investors
Study revealed as commissioned by a litigation lawyer with falsified patient data
Vaxxed film and Infowars appearances push a CDC cover-up claim
Sears put on probation by the California medical board in 2018

notes: Primary subject is the movement, so roles are empty; Wakefield and Sears each get a full part as secondary subjects. Transcript renders the activist as Laura Little; the usual spelling is Lora Little. Sears's birth year is not given, so left null. main_span starts at the first anti-vaccination society (about 1798) and stays open because the movement was active at release. No content warning: smallpox symptoms and child deaths are described briefly, not at length.
